problem_framing.reason: A1 separates the objective (whether public evidence justifies a consumer proposition) from the suggested solution. It lists real alternatives: a consumer proposition, a professional-line extension, no expansion, and a route-to-market change. It also requires value capture for Tennant. It does not reach rung 3. It flags no missed option or false premise. It also calls consumer reach unknown without examining the 'Sales direct to consumer' line in the 10-Q source, which the agent later retrieved (A4). The €20,000 / 12-week budget is an assumption, not an observed fact.

causal_mechanism.reason: The better theory, T1 (A9), names a benefit: premium margins from a lifestyle or status product. Its behaviour chain is not grounded. It assumes households will buy multiple floor-cleaning units because they are status symbols. It also says value is captured by 'leveraging its existing distribution network', but no source shows Tennant has retail consumer reach. T2 (A10) is internally incoherent: it claims consumers will 'accept lower prices' and pay less because items are essential, and will also buy multiple units.

distinct_theories.reason: T1 and T2 are near-templated copies. Both have the same structure, the same retail-plus-subscription channel and the same 'multiple units per household' mechanism. Their third predictions are word-for-word identical. They differ only in framing (status versus health) and price direction, not in product, customer or channel.

assumptions_predictions.reason: Some predictions are nominally observable, such as units per household and survey willingness to pay. They are vague, and they would not put the theories in trouble because they share the same retail-sales prediction. T2 predicts higher willingness to pay for essential models while assuming consumers pay lower prices for essentials, so its prediction contradicts its own assumption.

evidence_judgement.reason: Every assessment is 'neutral' and uses near-identical boilerplate 'does not show' text. The assessments mislabel the Nilfisk sources, which the packet classes as verified_observation, as company_assertion (A12, A14, A16). They never engage with the most relevant consumer-market evidence: the Tineco wet-dry segment and Kärcher's note that consumer demand was mixed. They state no limits on date, place or fit to the customer group, and never ask what 'Sales direct to consumer' in the 10-Q actually denotes.

seeking_challenge.reason: There is one challenge search against T1 (A13). Its results, including Tineco and the IR overview, are never reported or assessed, and nothing is searched against T2. This is a token look with no fair report of what was found.

experiment_design.reason: The run stopped at the turn limit (A18) before any test was proposed or declined.

revision.reason: Revision is excluded from packet.applicable_dimensions, and no update was scheduled.

recommendation.reason: The investigation stopped before giving any recommendation (A18).

red_flags.reason: The episode ended at the turn limit with no recommendation and no experiment stage.

No source supports the claims that consumers treat floor scrubbers as status items bought in multiples, or that Tennant's existing professional distribution network can serve retail consumers. T2's mechanism, where consumers 'accept lower prices' because items are essential and prefer them at higher willingness to pay, is incoherent.
Sources that the packet classes as verified_observation (Nilfisk) are mislabelled as company_assertion.
The rival theories share an identical retail-sales prediction, so it cannot discriminate between them.

judgment.screen_reason: Rejected. The episode is incomplete, with no recommendation or test stage (A18). It also contains material unsupported inference in both theories (A9, A10), misclassifies source types (A12, A14, A16), and gives near-duplicate theories with a non-discriminating shared prediction.
